extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide for appropriate language, terminology choices and reporting practices when covering people with disabilities and related topics. It gives background on terms, NCDJ recommendations and notes on AP style where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cretin
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical term used for people with congenital hypothyroidism; originally meant “wretch, innocent victim” or simply “Christian.” Once a neutral descriptor in some Romance dialects, it has been used as a slur to describe people with intellectual disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: “Cretin” is considered a slur to describe a person with intellectual disabilities. Use the term “hypothyroidism” instead. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripple/crip
rubrics_metrics.description: “Cripple” defined as a lame or partly disabled person or animal; historically used and became offensive in the early 20th century. Some disability activists have reclaimed the word; others find it offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “cripple” as either a noun or verb unless you are describing the “crip” movement or if it’s in a direct quote. AP style: “Cripple” is considered offensive when used to describe a person who is lame or disabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cued speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of hand signs and placements near the mouth used to differentiate between sounds while mouthing words; not interchangeable with sign language and not a sign language itself. It’s used to help children who are deaf or hard-of-hearing understand spoken languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Because it is not commonly used, particularly in the U.S., include a definition when using the term. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes a person with profound or complete hearing loss. Many consider deafness a culture rather than solely a disability. Some prefer lowercase 'deaf' for audiological status and uppercase 'Deaf' for the community/culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: “Deaf” or “hard of hearing” are the preferred terms. Uppercase when referring to the “Deaf” community and lowercase when referring to the condition. Avoid using “hearing impaired” or “partial” or “partially” in reference to deafness or hearing loss unless people use those terms for themselves. Ask about identity-first vs person-first language; National Association of the Deaf supports identity-first. When quoting/paraphrasing signed responses, indicate signed on first reference. AP style: Uses “deaf” for total hearing loss and “partially deaf” or “partial hearing loss” for others; uses lowercase 'd' in all usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf-blind / Deafblind / DeafBlind
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms indicating some loss of both vision and hearing; historically hyphenated (deaf-blind) but some organizations now use deafblind to reflect possibility of additional disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: The terms deafblind, deafblindness, deaf-blind and deaf-blindness are all acceptable. However, whenever possible, ask the individual which term they prefer. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf and dumb / deaf-mute
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical terms implying inability to speak; inaccurate and offensive because people with hearing loss can communicate in many ways and may be able to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid these terms as they often are used inaccurately and can be offensive. It is acceptable to refer to someone as deaf or hard of hearing. If possible, ask the person which is preferable. State specific communication methods (ASL, lip-reading, etc.) instead. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect / birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: “Defect” implies imperfection; a birth defect is a physical or biochemical difference present at birth. Many find ‘defect’ derogatory when describing people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “defect” or “defective” when describing a disability. Instead, state the nature of the disability or injury. AP style: “Birth defect” is acceptable in broad references but not when referring to a specific person or group; be specific and use only if relevant. Some prefer “congenital disorder.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformed / deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity denotes body parts not having the typical shape; term has negative connotations when used to describe people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “deformed” as an adjective to describe a person. AP style: AP medical stories tend to refer to a specific deformity rather than calling an individual “deformed.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Dementia / senility
rubrics_metrics.description: Dementia is an umbrella term for cognitive decline severe enough to interfere with daily life, with Alzheimer’s as the most common form. Terms like “demented” or “senile” are often inaccurate and stigmatizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having dementia only if relevant and you are confident there is a medical diagnosis. Use “a person with dementia” rather than “demented” or “senile.” When possible, reference the specific disease (e.g., Huntington’s, Parkinson’s) and use full disease names. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depression
rubrics_metrics.description: Major depressive disorder characterized by prolonged mood/functional changes; includes related diagnoses like seasonal affective disorder, psychotic depression and postpartum depression. Bipolar disorder formerly called manic-depressive illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having depression only if relevant and you’re confident there is a medical diagnosis. If no diagnosis, use quotes and state diagnosis unconfirmed. Specify type if known. Terms like “depressed,” “depressing” are acceptable in non-diagnostic contexts. AP style: Suggests naming the specific condition when possible; use lowercase unless referring to the Great Depression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental disabilities / disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental disabilities are conditions arising during the developmental period (before age 22) that impact daily functioning and often last a lifetime (examples: autism, spina bifida, cerebral palsy, intellectual disabilities). Legal definitions vary by state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Acceptable to use “developmental disability/developmental disabilities,” but prefer naming the specific disability when possible. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differently-abled
rubrics_metrics.description: Term from the 1990s intended as an alternative to 'disabled' or 'handicapped'; many consider it condescending or evasive and not appropriate for referring to individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: “Person with a disability” is a more neutral term than “differently-abled.” AP style: Suggests avoiding the term and being specific about the disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled / disability
rubrics_metrics.description: General terms describing functional limitations affecting major life activities; legal definitions vary. Reminder that people with disabilities are not monolithic and should not be referred to as a single undifferentiated group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Usually acceptable to use these terms, but avoid referring to “the disabled.” Do not reference disabilities unless pertinent to the story; prefer specific condition names when possible. AP style: “Disabled” is a general term; avoid “handicapped.” See related entries on phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability studies
rubrics_metrics.description: An interdisciplinary academic field that examines disability within humanities, social sciences and other perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use Disability Studies like other academic disciplines. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled people / people with disabilities (identity-first vs person-first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity-first (e.g., 'autistic') vs people-first (e.g., 'person with autism') language preferences vary by community and geography. Some groups (UK, some US activists) prefer identity-first language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Ask the person or organization spokesperson about preferred terminology. Conforms to AP style, which advises person-first language when describing groups or when preferences are unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disfigurement / disfigured
rubrics_metrics.description: Disfigurement refers to physical changes caused by burns, trauma, disease or congenital conditions; term can be derogatory when applied to people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Do not call someone “disfigured”; refer specifically to the physical changes. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissociative identity disorder / multiple personality disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more distinct personality states (‘alters’) and related symptoms like memory loss and disorientation. 'Multiple personality disorder' is outdated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having “dissociative identity disorder” only if relevant and you are confident of a medical diagnosis. Use the term “dissociative identity disorder,” not “multiple personality disorder,” and avoid the acronym “DID.” AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversabled / Diversability
rubrics_metrics.description: A branded term/movement (coined by Tiffany Yu) to frame disability as part of diversity and to celebrate disability pride and empowerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: When referring to Tiffany Yu’s group use “Diversability” as a proper name. Otherwise, use “disabled,” “disability” or “person with a disability.” AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Down syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: A congenital condition caused by an extra full or partial copy of chromosome 21 (Trisomy 21) with physical and cognitive characteristics; historically called 'mongoloidism' which is offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Proper term is Down syndrome (not Down’s). Avoid “suffers from” or “afflicted with.” Terms like “intellectually disabled,” “developmentally disabled,” “cognitive disability” are acceptable in people-first contexts, but it is more accurate to name Down syndrome when that is the diagnosis. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dwarf / little person / midget / short stature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwarfism is a medical/genetic condition resulting in stature below ~4'10"; 'midget' is derogatory; 'little people' and 'little person' are commonly used but preferences vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Only refer to short stature if relevant; ask people which term they prefer. Use “dwarf” only when referring to a medical diagnosis or in a quote. Avoid “vertically challenged” and “midget.” AP style: “Dwarf” preferred for medical/genetic condition; “midget” is offensive; plural is “dwarfs.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Dyslexia / dyslexic
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning disability with difficulties in phonological processing, spelling, reading and related tasks; used as noun/adjective by some but noun use is falling out of favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having dyslexia only if relevant and confident of a medical diagnosis. If no diagnosis, use quotes and indicate unconfirmed. Ask people how they want to be described; some prefer 'dyslexic', others prefer people-first phrasing. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilepsy / epileptic / epileptic fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronic neurological condition characterized by recurrent unprovoked seizures; severity and manifestations vary widely. Not all seizures indicate epilepsy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to someone as having epilepsy only if relevant and you are confident of a medical diagnosis. Avoid calling someone “an epileptic”; prefer “has epilepsy” or “has been diagnosed with epilepsy.” Use “seizure” rather than “fit” or “epileptic fit.” AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitated communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A discredited technique from the 1990s where a facilitator purportedly helps nonverbal people communicate; academic studies found little evidence it works and often attribute output to the aide rather than the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid language that may legitimize facilitated communication. When writing about it, specify that major disability organizations do not recognize it as valid. AP style: Not addressed. Note: distinguish facilitated communication from legitimate augmentative and alternative communication methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freak / freak show
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically used to describe people with physical oddities in sideshows; derogatory when applied to people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Do not use “freak” to describe a person with a disability as it is derogatory. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic defect / genetic disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Genetic disorder caused by DNA changes (single-gene, multifactorial, chromosomal). Genetic conditions are congenital but not all congenital conditions are genetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid terms like “disorder” or “defect” which can be derogatory; use “condition” unless referring to specific medical diagnosis. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifted / twice exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: Giftedness indicates capacity to perform above peers; twice-exceptional (2E) refers to someone identified as gifted and also having a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid describing people as “gifted” or “twice exceptional” unless identified as such by a professional. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handicap / handicapped / handicapable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Handicap” historically used for physical disability; fallen out of favor. “Handicapable” was coined as a positive alternative but is not widely accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “handicap” and “handicapped” when describing a person; instead use specific condition or “person with a disability.” Terms are acceptable when citing laws or places (e.g., handicapped parking) though “accessible parking” is preferred. Avoid “handicapable.” Conforms to AP style regarding “handicap” and “handicapped.” AP style: Does not address “handicapable.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard of hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to hearing conditions that can be helped by an auditory device; some with mild/moderate loss may affiliate with Deaf community and prefer 'deaf'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: “Hard of hearing” is almost always acceptable; use preferred term if possible. AP style: Not addressed except to recommend using “hard of hearing” without hyphens unless it is an adjective directly preceding a person (AP advises against the latter formulation). See also Deaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing impaired / hearing impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms describing hearing loss; often disliked because they frame people in terms of deficiency. World Federation of the Deaf views “hearing impaired” as unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “hearing impaired” or “hearing impairment.” For total hearing loss, use “deaf”; otherwise “hard of hearing.” Ask sources for preference. AP style: Defers to National Association of the Deaf: “hearing-impaired” was well-meaning but is not accepted/used by many deaf and hard of hearing people. See also Deaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: High functioning / low functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels used to denote ability levels across neurodiversity, intellectual disability and mental illness; considered reductive and dismissive by many advocates and not medical diagnoses (e.g., “high-functioning autism”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “high functioning” and “low functioning.” Instead, use medical diagnoses and describe specific abilities and challenges. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homebound / housebound
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms meaning confined to the home; can be misapplied to people who use mobility assistance but are independent. Veterans Affairs has specific definition for housebound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using the terms unless in a direct quote. AP style: Not addressed except to state that homebound and housebound are one word with no hyphens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that places the disability first (e.g., 'autistic person') as opposed to people-first (e.g., 'person with autism'). Preferences vary by community; Deaf and many autistic people prefer identity-first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Ask the person with the disability how they want to be described. If not possible, ask an organizational spokesperson for preferred terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impaired / impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like “hearing impairment” or “visually impaired” are widely used medically and legally but are criticized for implying deficiency; impairment refers to organ/structure condition, disability refers to functional limitation caused by impairment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: When possible, avoid describing a person or condition as “impaired.” See alternative language under specific entries (hearing, visual). AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantile paralysis / poliomyelitis / polio / post-polio syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Infantile paralysis is an older term for poliomyelitis (polio). Post-polio syndrome affects some who had polio long after recovery, with new muscle weakness and fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use the term polio rather than infantile paralysis. Prefer phrases like “He had polio as a child,” or “He has post-polio syndrome” rather than “He suffers from polio” or “He is a victim of polio.” Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury / injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: “Injury” describes harm from accidents or events; common phrasing includes 'injuries suffered in a car accident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Refer to injuries as being “sustained” or “received” rather than “suffered,” because “suffer” implies victimhood or diminishment. AP style: The stylebook allows injuries may be “suffered,” “sustained” or “received.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane / insanity / mentally deranged / psychopathology
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal terms used to denote mental instability; can be offensive and imprecise. 'Insanity' is a legal question in criminal law, not a medical diagnosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use “mental illness” instead of “insane” or “mentally deranged,” except in quotes or when referring to a criminal defense. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane asylum / mental health hospital / psychiatric hospital
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic term 'insane asylum' is outdated and objectionable; modern facilities should be described with clinical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Use “behavioral health hospital” or “psychiatric hospital” to describe medical facilities devoted to mental health treatment. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual disabilities / intellectually disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual disability involves significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior; debates exist about the role of IQ testing in diagnosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Both terms are acceptable, though many prefer people-first phrasing (a person with an intellectual disability). Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used by some to refer to couples where one partner has a disability and the other does not; intended to destigmatize such relationships but usage is not widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Because the term is not in widespread use, explain its meaning for general audiences and ask sources how they prefer to describe their relationships. AP style: Only reference relates to hyphenation; use interabled (no hyphen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Older term for a person weakened or disabled by illness; considered offensive and inaccurate because it implies lack of ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Avoid using “invalid” to describe a person with a disability except in direct quotes. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many disabilities are not outwardly visible (chronic illnesses, mental illness, hearing loss without devices, etc.); public assumptions about visible markers of disability are often inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ Recommendation: Do not apply the term “invisible disability” to people without asking their preference. Many with chronic illnesses do not consider themselves disabled and may be offended by the term.
